new_statements.quote: [p.47] In addition to these two basic tones, there is also a phonologically significant Downstep ... Lower Cross languages can therefore be characterized as being two-toned, terraced level languages. [p.55] ... it is difficult to find any true evidence for stress, at least in the sense proposed by Ward32. [fn.32] This is not to assert that there is no stress at all in Efik or the other LC languages. There is likely some sort phrasal stress, and also the juncture between elements of compound words appears to be marked by stress, but these are clearly not what Ward was referring to. [fn.34] ... as the foot is a notion usually associated with stress phenomena, it is by no means clear how it would apply in a non-stress language.
new_statements.citation: Connell, Bruce A. 1991. Phonetic aspects of the Lower Cross languages and their implications for sound change. PhD thesis, University of Edinburgh.
new_statements.locator: sec. 2.2.2 'Tone', p.47 (PDF p.61); sec. 2.3.3.3 pp.54-55 with fn.32 p.55 (PDF p.69); fn.34 p.56 (PDF p.70). Ibuoro listed as a sampled language p.5 (PDF p.19).
new_statements.rule_in_words: All Lower Cross languages, Ibuoro included (one of the 19 sampled), are two-tone (H, L) terraced-level tone languages with contrastive downstep; Connell finds no true evidence for word stress (rejecting Ward's 1933 verb-root stress for Efik), allows only probable phrasal stress and stress-like marking at compound junctures, and treats LC as 'non-stress' languages. The statement is group-level; nothing Ibuoro-specific is said about prosody beyond its inclusion in the sample and (Connell 1994 p.10) its lesser degree of H-spread falling tones.
new_statements.exceptions: Faraclas (1984a,b) argues for a third (extra-high) tone and phrasal stress in Obolo; compound-word junctures 'appear to be marked by stress'; consonant weakening by word position 'may be related to stress in Ibibio... which to date remains unstudied' (p.104).
new_statements.domain_note: Group-level characterization of Lower Cross lexical items in citation form (tone) and of Efik/LC generally (stress); explicitly leaves phrasal stress open. Not an Ibuoro-specific description; Ibuoro data in the thesis are consonant inventories and tone-marked wordlist rows only.
new_statements.identity_note: The quoted statements are group-level for the Lower Cross languages (Glottolog obol1242 'Lower Cross'), argued mainly from Efik and Ibibio; Ibuoro (ibuo1242, alt. name Iwerre; Connell's 'Ibuoro (Iwerre - Akwa Ibom)') is one of the 19 languages in Connell's sample but receives no language-specific prosodic description. Connell 1994 p.5 treats Ibuoro, Itu Mbon Uso (itum1245), Nkari (nkar1234) and possibly Ito (itoo1242) as a possible dialect cluster (Glottolog node ibuo1243). No Ibuoro-specific phonology, grammar or thesis exists in any index reached.

sources.citation: Connell, Bruce. 1994. The Lower Cross languages: a prolegomena to the classification of the Cross River languages. Journal of West African Languages 24(1): 3-46.
sources.note: Ibuoro in sample (p.4-6, 9). Sec. 3.3 p.10: 'in all languages of the group, there are two tones, high (H) and low (L), and contrastive downstep (D)'; Ibuoro 'affected to a lesser degree' by H-spread falling tones. Sec. 5 p.12: tonal systems 'further complicated through interaction with phrasal stress, but except for Faraclas (1984b) for Obolo, no investigation in this area has been done.' No word-stress statement.
